thread.title: Palo Alto: Growth At A Premium - Palo Alto Networks (NYSE:PANW) | Seeking Alpha

author: Hervé Blandin
title: Palo Alto: Growth At A Premium - Palo Alto Networks (NYSE:PANW) | Seeking Alpha
text:
Without any doubt, Palo Alto (NYSE: PANW ) has been growing revenues strongly over the past few years. Better than words, the slide below proves it.
(Source: Investor Day Presentation 2017 )
A revenue CAGR of 47% in a market CAGR of 7% deserves respect and admiration. As a consequence, the market share of the company is growing, not only in the traditional security market but also in the endpoint security and web security areas, as shown in the two slides below.
(Source: Investor Day Presentation 2017)
(Source: Investor Day Presentation 2017)
Palo Alto should keep on gaining market share, as management forecasts 27% revenue growth for fiscal 2018.
The market seems to appreciate these results with a market cap of more than $19 billion.
(Source: Seeking Alpha )
In this article, I try to understand what makes the company so successful by taking a closer look at its business and financial statements.
Which products drive Palo Alto's success? Palo Alto describes its products as a "Next-Generation Security Platform" with three elements that interact with each other: next-generation firewalls, an endpoint protection software, and a threat intelligence cloud solution. These types of products are also proposed by other security vendors, such as Check Point Software Technologies (NASDAQ: CHKP ).
However, the concept of platform is expanding with a new interesting feature that the company calls "Application Framework". It allows third-party developers to propose security apps leveraging the Palo Alto solution. A comparison with the Apple Store (NASDAQ: AAPL ) comes to mind.
In the Q3 2018 conference call, management indicated that it did not intend to monetize the Application Framework in the short term; customers would buy apps directly to the providers of these apps. Palo Alto would monetize the application framework when its ecosystem becomes important. For instance, the company could take a commission on the third-party application sales.
I imagine that the niche security players would be attracted by this proposition, allowing them to sell a security solution without physically installing any device on the customer side, leveraging the existing Palo Alto infrastructure.
According to the company, the application framework would create a $5 billion market by 2020, in addition to the estimated $24 billion market.
(Source: Company Presentation Q3 2018 )
I doubt that the application framework would create an additional market. A company that would buy an application in the scope of the application framework would have bought an equivalent solution somewhere else if the framework would not exist. However, if successful, the application framework would increase Palo Alto's market share.
Although innovative and attractive, the security solution proposed by Palo Alto is not unique and cannot explain by itself the impressive growing market share. The application framework is a real innovation that will officially be released in August 2018 and has not contributed to any growth yet. We'll see below that the growth could also be linked with high sales and marketing expenses.
What's happening on the financial side? As highlighted in the income statement below, the revenue growth comes at the price of high operating expenses at more than 80% of revenues. Sales and marketing expenses, with 50% of the revenues, largely contribute to the costs.
(Source: Company Annual Report 2017 )
High sales and marketing expenses might be due to high commissions distributed to partners, providing them a superior incentive to sell a Palo Alto solution against another vendor. For instance, or Check Point Software spent respectively 20% and 23% in sales and marketing in 2017. Should the Palo Alto sales and marketing expenses come in line with competitors (representing a reduction of $500 million), growth would slow down.
In addition, GAAP net income stays negative. However, the company highlights only positive results, as shown on the slide below.
(Source: Company Presentation Q3 2018)
We can see two interesting figures:
The operating margins gravitate at about 20%, while the income statement shows losses. High share-based compensation (SBC), which the company does not take into account when calculating margins, explains the discrepancy. The FCF margin stay above 37%, while the company has been showing GAAP operating losses. The recognition of revenues for multi-year contracts justifies this difference. I detail these two aspects in the following paragraphs.
Margins and share-based compensation In addition to highlighting 20% operating margins, the company has created another slide (below) showing the benefits of its scale regarding the operating margin. I have highlighted the numbers to pay attention to.
(Source: Company Presentation Q3 2018)
None of these figures take into account SBC, which is a real cost. Even GAAP accounting agrees with me on this.
When taking into account SBC, the leverage is going the opposite way, with a -10.2% GAAP operating margin in 2017 against a 1.5% GAAP operating margin in 2012, as shown on the table below. (I have highlighted the relevant numbers.)
(Source: Company Presentation Q3 2018, annexes)
The same principle applies for the gross and free cash flow margins.
Not considering SBC when highlighting margins is misleading, especially when SBC compensation represents an important part of expenses. With $475.7 million of SBC and 4,562 employees in fiscal 2017, employees received on average more than $100,000 of SBC. Management indicated in the Q3 2018 10-Q that SBC was expected to continue constituting an important part of the expenses, being at least $920 million over the next 2.6 years.
On a side note, in 2017, Palo Alto has started to repurchase $420.1 million worth of shares. The amount is slightly lower than SBC. It confirms, if it was necessary, that SBC is a real cost: the share buyback drains $420.1 million of cash from the company just to slow down the dilution to shareholders due to SBC.
And now, the FCF story The deferred revenues have been growing, as shown on the graph below. It does not say anything about profitability, but at least it shows that billing is growing faster than recognition of revenues.
(Source: Company Presentation Q3 2018)
When billing is growing, Palo Alto receives more cash than the revenues it recognizes in its income statement. The idea of this revenue accounting rule is to match revenues with costs in order to better reflect the reality.
In the meantime, the company has chosen to communicate about the FCF, as shown on the slide below, with impressive FCF margins under different growth scenarios.
(Source: Investor Day Presentation 2017)
The company calculates the FCF as shown on the table below.
(Source: Company Annual Report 2017)
The net cash provided by operating activities takes into account the deferred revenues (which is cash) and does not take into account SBC (which is not cash). That makes sense because net cash provided by operating activities is all about cash.
Therefore, the FCF margin shows an optimistic picture of the company. The FCF calculation does not take into account SBC, and does not consider the associated costs related to the recognition of the deferred revenues. For instance, Palo Alto allocates commission costs to vendors in proportion to the recognized revenues, and this is not reflected in the FCF calculation. In addition, the actual service the customers pay for generates real costs for the company (maintenance, opex, etc.).
SBC amounted to $475.7 million in 2017, and we don't know the costs corresponding to the recognition of the deferred revenues.
In any case, it means that after taking into account SBC only, FCF drops below $705.1 million - $475.7 million = $230 million in 2017, which corresponds to an FCF margin below 13%. This is quite different from a 37%+ FCF margin.
Management remuneration As a bonus, let's have a look at the management remuneration, summarized in the table below.
(Source: Palo Alto Proxy 2017 )
For comparison, the table below shows the remuneration for the management of Arista (NYSE: ANET ), a comparable high-tech company, created at about the same time, with similar revenues, growth profile, market size, and market capitalization.
The main difference is that Palo Alto is involved in the network security business, while Arista's activity is related to the cloud data center network.
(Source: Arista Proxy 2017 )
The table below shows another comparison with Fortinet (NASDAQ: FTNT ), a security company with similar sales and slower growth.
(Source: Fortinet Proxy 2017 )
Palo Alto seems to pay its management very well. The table below presents the insider share transactions over the last 12 months.
(Source: Dataroma.com )
The only buyer of the $20 million worth of shares is the new CEO, Nikesh Arora, who started in June 2018.
According to the 2017 proxy, the variable remuneration of the management is based on the billing and non-GAAP EPS, which does not take into account the share-based compensation (what a surprise!). I think it is safe to assume that SBC will still be an important part of the payroll in order to drive billing growth.
Valuation I assume that Palo Alto market share keeps on growing by 7.3% during the next five years, as it did during the last five years. The market could amount to $27.5 billion by 2022.
Palo Alto market share would reach 16.5%, and revenues would represent $4.54 billion. While real FCF margins are currently below 13%, I assume an FCF margin at 20% due to bigger scale. That would represent $0.9 billion of FCF in 2022. At a market cap minus cash of $17 billion, the market values the company at 19x FCF in 5 years with optimistic assumptions.
Considering the remuneration policy of management, which I estimate not being aligned with shareholders, the high sales and marketing expenses, the misleading communication, and the risk of dilution, I would not want to own Palo Alto shares at this price or even lower.
Risks and opportunities A new high-profile CEO has started in June 2018, and he purchased $20 million of shares. The application framework seems to be a real innovation in the security space, but assessing its potential is challenging. Convertible debt, warrants, and SBC will dilute shareholders. Over the last few years, Palo Alto has acquired several companies. In addition to the integration risks, it has added goodwill to the balance sheet. The company evolves in a highly technological environment and must keep up with innovation. Revenue and billing growth relies on high sales and marketing expenses. Conclusion Palo Alto has been growing faster than its competitors with its security platform. However, share-based compensation and deferred revenues accounting makes the company less attractive than presented by management.
The market seems to value the company at a premium. Taking into account the risks involved, I don't plan to own PANW shares, even at a lower price.
Disclosure: I/we have no positions in any stocks mentioned, and no plans to initiate any positions within the next 72 hours.
